lesson.menu_desc: Risk out loud: what happens if they sign, and what would happen if the clause came out
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- If This Goes Through
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Amanda Merlini | Lesson 4 -- If This Goes Through

vocab.title: Match each expression to its meaning
defs: a private way of deciding a dispute, outside the courts
to promise to pay for a loss that the other side suffers
the honest intention to keep the agreement, even where it says nothing
to leave a negotiation without a deal
to end a contract early, using a right the contract gives you
the point where neither side will move and the talk stops
the legal responsibility to pay when something goes wrong
the part of the contract that says how much a late or failed delivery costs

items.situation: The commercial team asks: "What happens if they sign on Friday?"
tips: If they sign on Friday, the first shipment will leave in three weeks.
Real and likely: if + present, then will.

items.situation: They ask: "And what would happen if we took the penalty clause out?"
tips: If we took it out, we would have no number to claim when a shipment is late.

items.situation: The buyer asks you to accept unlimited liability.
tips: I am afraid we cannot. If our liability were unlimited, no insurer would cover the contract.
Refuse, then give the consequence. Never the other way round.

items.situation: Your director asks: "Is arbitration better than court for us?"
tips: If we choose arbitration, the case will be faster and private, but it will cost more at the start.
One sentence with both sides of the trade-off.

items.situation: The other side says: "Take it or leave it."
tips: If that is your final position, we will have to walk away. I would rather find a middle point today.
Name the consequence calmly, then open a door.

items.situation: The talk has reached a deadlock and everybody is tired.
tips: If we parked this clause and came back to it tomorrow, we would both think more clearly.
The second conditional is how you propose without pressing.

listenings.text: Amanda, this is Henrik, counsel for the buyer. I am sending you our comments before tomorrow so that the call is short. Three points. First, the penalty clause. Two per cent a week is too high for us; if we accept that number, our own insurance premium goes up, and the commercial team will not sign. Second, liability. We would like a cap, and the cap we have in mind is the value of the shipment, not the value of the whole contract. Third, and this one is easier, arbitration. If you agree to London, we agree to the rest of the dispute section as it stands. I want to be honest with you: on the first two we have room to move, on the cap we have very little. See you tomorrow at ten.

Hi Amanda, it is Karin from risk. I looked at the position sheet you sent, and here is where we are before you go into that call. On the penalty, anything above one per cent a week is fine for us, because the insurer covers the difference. On the liability cap, that is the one I worry about. If we cap it at the value of one shipment, a serious quality problem would cost us five times what we could claim, so I would not go there without the finance director. On arbitration, London is acceptable, but do not give it away for free: if they want London, ask for something on the penalty in exchange. And one last thing. If they walk away, we still have the other buyer, so you are not negotiating from a weak position. Good luck tomorrow.

extra_audio.text: Say what the clause does today, in one sentence. Then say what will happen if the other side signs it as it is. Then say what would happen if the clause came out. Then say which risk your company can live with, and which one it cannot. And finally, propose the exchange: what you can give, and what you want back.
